name: Somatrogon
lead: Somatrogon (code name MOD-4023; brand name Ngenla) is a long-acting recombinant human growth hormone analogue given as a once-weekly subcutaneous injection. It is a prescription medicine used to support growth in children whose bodies do not make enough growth hormone. For a child with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency (GHD), the aim is to restore the hormone signal that drives bone growth, so that growth velocity rises and the child's height moves toward the expected range for their age and family [9][8]. For height, this is the mechanism: replace the missing hormone, raise IGF-1, speed growth of the long bones while growth plates are still open, and reach a taller adult height than the deficiency would otherwise allow [9][27].

The drug is designed to reduce the injection burden of standard growth hormone therapy, which is normally a daily injection. Somatrogon links short segments of the human chorionic gonadotropin tail to the growth hormone molecule, which slows its clearance and allows weekly rather than daily dosing [17]. In the US it is indicated for children aged 3 years and older with growth failure due to inadequate secretion of endogenous growth hormone [9].

Phase 3 trials compared weekly somatrogon with daily somatropin in prepubertal children with GHD, and reviews of the long-acting growth hormones (lonapegsomatropin, somatrogon and somapacitan) describe height velocity comparable to daily growth hormone over 52 weeks, with similar safety profiles [1][2][4]. It is a prescription medicine for a diagnosed deficiency; no completed study has tested it for height gain in children without a diagnosed deficiency, although a trial in children born small for gestational age or with idiopathic short stature has been registered [10].

In height-focused online circles, growth hormone in general is a frequent topic and long-acting products are sometimes asked about for convenience. The research and the label concern children with a diagnosed deficiency under specialist care; the question of whether growth hormone adds height in children who make normal amounts is studied under other indications such as idiopathic short stature, and a trial of somatrogon in that group is registered but not completed [10][28].

sections.h: Background: growth hormone deficiency and daily therapy
paras: Growth hormone deficiency in children is often of unknown cause; other causes include gene mutations, pituitary malformations, tumours near the pituitary and head injury. Wikipedia notes that growth is usually normal in the first months of life and that poor growth becomes apparent later in infancy, with puberty and bone maturation often delayed [27]. Because growth hormone is released in bursts, a single blood level is not diagnostic; clinicians combine growth measurements, IGF-1 levels and stimulation tests that look at the response to agents such as arginine, clonidine or glucagon [27].

Until the 1980s, growth hormone for children came from human pituitary glands collected after death: about 7,700 US children and 27,000 worldwide received it between 1963 and 1985. After four young adults who had received it developed Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in 1985, its use stopped, and Genentech's recombinant growth hormone (Protropin) was introduced that year [29]. Recombinant daily injection then became the standard of care, which is the regimen long-acting products were designed to relieve [29][20].

Treated children typically begin growing faster within months; growth often slows later but remains above the normal rate, so a child who fell far behind may reach the normal height range over several years, according to Wikipedia's summary [27]. Children are monitored every 3 to 6 months and usually continue treatment while they are growing [27].

The US label indicates somatrogon for pediatric patients aged 3 years and older who have growth failure due to inadequate secretion of endogenous growth hormone [9]. It has also been approved in Canada, Australia, Japan, the European Union and the UK [17]. Wikipedia lists the Australian approval as November 2021, the European approval as February 2022 and the US approval as June 2023 [16].

Growth hormone deficiency is diagnosed by endocrinologists using growth measurements, bone age and hormone testing; the product is prescribed within that setting. Adults with GHD have also been studied: a randomised phase 3 study of once-weekly somatrogon in adults has been published [22].

Three weekly products were approved between 2020 and 2023 using different designs. Somapacitan (Sogroya, Novo Nordisk) carries a component that binds reversibly to serum albumin; it was approved in the US in August 2020 first for adults with growth hormone deficiency [30]. Lonapegsomatropin (Skytrofa, Ascendis Pharma) is a prodrug of somatropin approved in the US in August 2021 and in the EU in January 2022 [31]. Somatrogon (Pfizer and OPKO Health) adds segments of the human chorionic gonadotropin tail to growth hormone, and was approved in Canada, Australia, the EU and, in June 2023, the US [8][16][17].

Comparative work is indirect because the products were tested in separate trials. The network meta-analysis and the systematic review cited under Clinical studies found comparable 52-week height velocity across the long-acting products and daily growth hormone [3][18].

The manufacturer describes Ngenla as a prefilled once-weekly pen in two strengths, with the dose chosen by the prescribing doctor, a low injection volume and a fine needle, and no reconstitution step; it is given on the same day each week [32]. The brand's safety information lists contraindications including closed growth plates, active cancer or tumours, diabetes-related eye problems, and certain critical illnesses, and cautions for Prader-Willi syndrome with severe obesity or sleep apnoea [32].

Serious risks named by the manufacturer include increased risk of death in critically ill children, serious allergic reactions, tumour growth or recurrence, high blood sugar or diabetes, raised pressure inside the skull, fluid retention, lower cortisol or thyroid hormone, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, worsening scoliosis, pancreatitis, and loss of fat tissue at injection sites; common side effects of 5 percent or more include injection-site reactions, colds, headache, fever, anaemia, cough and vomiting [32]. Wikipedia lists its legal status as prescription-only in the US, EU, Canada and Australia [16][16].

According to the label, somatrogon binds the growth hormone receptor and activates the STAT5b signalling pathway, increasing serum IGF-1; GH and IGF-1 then drive metabolic changes and linear growth [9].

Somatrogon is a glycoprotein that uses three copies of the C-terminal peptide of human chorionic gonadotropin to delay clearance, which is what permits a weekly schedule [17]. Other long-acting products reach the same goal differently: lonapegsomatropin is a prodrug and somapacitan carries an albumin-binding attachment [4][17]. A cross-over study has examined the comparability of two drug product presentations of somatrogon-ghla [24].

Somatrogon was developed by OPKO Health and Pfizer. Its pivotal phase 3 trial began in December 2016 [13]. It received its first approval in October 2021 in Canada [8], and the US FDA review of the application was extended in September 2021 before the June 2023 US approval, per press releases summarised on Wikipedia [16]. Reviews place it alongside lonapegsomatropin (FDA approved in August 2021) and somapacitan as the first generation of weekly growth hormones [4].

Daily injection has long been the standard of care for pediatric GHD, and adherence to daily regimens can be difficult for families; this is the motivation reviewers cite for weekly products [20][17].

The most common reactions reported in the product information include injection-site reactions, headache and fever [16]. The US labels for long-acting growth hormones list warnings including increased mortality in acute critical illness, severe hypersensitivity, increased risk of neoplasms (notably second neoplasms in childhood cancer survivors), glucose intolerance and diabetes mellitus, intracranial hypertension, fluid retention, hypoadrenalism and hypothyroidism [9]. Label pregnancy information notes that no human data are available, and that rat reproduction studies showed no embryo-fetal toxicity [9].

sections.h: Idiopathic short stature and other height questions
paras: Idiopathic short stature (ISS) describes extreme shortness with no diagnosed explanation after a routine growth evaluation. One proposed definition, put forward when Eli Lilly sought FDA approval for its growth hormone in 2003, is height more than 2.25 standard deviations below the mean, around the shortest 1.2 percent of the population [28]. The approval of daily growth hormone for ISS drew criticism from some paediatric endocrinologists about treating short stature with normal test results as a disease, and definitions and treatment thresholds remain debated [29][28].

Somatrogon's approved indication is GHD only. A phase 3 comparison with daily Genotropin in children born small for gestational age or with ISS is registered [10]. Wikipedia's growth hormone therapy article adds that the New England Journal of Medicine in 2003 published editorials stating there was no evidence that growth hormone is safe or effective for healthy adults seeking anti-ageing effects, and that internet markets for products labelled HGH amplified unregulated sales [29].

In the global phase 3 study, 228 prepubertal children with GHD (boys aged 3-11, girls 3-10, no prior growth hormone treatment) were randomised to weekly somatrogon or daily somatropin for 12 months. Annualised height velocity at month 12 was 10.10 cm per year with somatrogon and 9.78 cm per year with somatropin, a difference of 0.33 cm per year (95% CI -0.24 to 0.89), which met the pre-specified non-inferiority margin [1]. A post hoc analysis looked at the Asian children in that study [23].

A Japanese phase 3 study randomised 44 prepubertal children to somatrogon or daily Genotropin [2][12], and an open-label extension followed Japanese children for up to four years [21]. A five-year open-label extension of a phase 2 dose-finding study has also been published [5]. A treatment-burden study of 87 children compared weekly and daily injections from the patient and caregiver perspective; 85 completed it [6][11]. A survey of investigators with experience of both regimens examined physician preference [20].

Pooled analyses are consistent with comparable growth. One meta-analysis of 16 efficacy and safety studies found no significant difference in annualised height velocity between long-acting and daily products; the somatrogon versus Genotropin difference was -1.40 cm per year with a confidence interval spanning zero (-2.91 to 0.10), while the TransCon product showed a small advantage over Genotropin [3]. A network meta-analysis found no differences at 52 weeks between somapacitan, somatrogon and lonapegsomatropin [18], and another network analysis compared the long-acting class with daily growth hormone [7]. Reviews note that long-term surveillance studies are still needed [17].

Trials of somatrogon in children without a diagnosed deficiency are at an early stage: a phase 3 comparison with Genotropin in children born small for gestational age or with idiopathic short stature is registered and recruiting [10]. Post-marketing surveillance in Korea and Japan and a study in India are registered [14][15][26].

Growth hormone is widely discussed in height-focused online communities, where some members ask about long-acting formulations for convenience, and about cost: a pen of a specialty biologic is expensive, and the product is sold through specialty pharmacies. Somatrogon is a prescription biologic for diagnosed deficiency, and its approved use is under specialist supervision [9][32].

Reviews of long-acting growth hormones describe their potential to improve adherence and quality of life as the main expected benefit over daily regimens; a treatment-burden study of 87 children compared weekly and daily injections from the child and caregiver point of view [17][25][6].

Cost has been a recurring theme in the growth hormone field. Wikipedia reports that early recombinant growth hormone cost roughly 10,000 to 30,000 US dollars a year at launch and that later competition lowered prices [29].

lore.intro: Growth hormone products are a recurring topic in height-focused communities, usually in the context of whether any hormone therapy can add height outside a diagnosed deficiency.

claims.claim: A weekly growth hormone pen is a more convenient way to raise IGF-1 and add height
claims.believers: Members of height communities see weekly dosing as removing the main burden of daily injections.
claims.experts: Weekly dosing is studied in children with diagnosed deficiency, where height velocity is comparable to daily somatropin over a year; reviews describe lower injection burden as the main expected benefit [1][17][25].

claims.claim: Growth hormone adds height in people who are not deficient
claims.believers: Some forum members treat growth hormone as a general height tool.
claims.experts: Wikipedia's summaries describe idiopathic short stature as the contested indication and note disagreement among endocrinologists; somatrogon itself has no completed trial outside GHD [28][29][10].

claims.claim: Growth hormone can add height after the growth plates close
claims.believers: Some communities discuss using it as an adult for height or body composition.
claims.experts: The manufacturer lists closed growth plates as a reason not to use the pediatric product [32].

claims.claim: Growth hormone is safe at any dose as a natural hormone
claims.believers: Growth hormone is described as a natural hormone with few risks.
claims.experts: The label and manufacturer information list neoplasm risk, glucose intolerance, intracranial hypertension, scoliosis progression and other warnings, and the 2011 FDA communication on mortality was inconclusive per Wikipedia [9][32][29].

claims.claim: Weekly products grow children as well as daily ones
claims.believers: Families and clinicians cite fewer injections as the appeal of weekly dosing.
claims.experts: A phase 3 randomised trial found non-inferior height velocity (10.10 vs 9.78 cm per year), and a network meta-analysis found no differences at 52 weeks [1][18].

card.summary: A weekly prescription growth hormone for children with diagnosed GH deficiency; no evidence for height gain without a deficiency.
card.note: Prescription drug for diagnosed GHD; trials are in children with deficiency only.

quick.overview:
Somatrogon (Ngenla) is a once-weekly growth hormone injection approved in the US for children aged 3 and older whose bodies do not make enough growth hormone. Phase 3 trials compared it with daily somatropin.

Trials involve children with a diagnosed deficiency. No study has tested it for height in children without one.
quick.mechanism: It binds the growth hormone receptor, activates STAT5b signalling and raises IGF-1, promoting linear growth.
quick.risks: The label lists warnings such as neoplasm risk, glucose intolerance, intracranial hypertension, fluid retention, hypoadrenalism, hypothyroidism and hypersensitivity. It is prescription-only.

chain: Weekly injection replaces missing growth hormone signal
Raises IGF-1 and growth velocity in children with GHD
Growth during childhood proceeds closer to expected, supporting final adult height
angle.text: In children with a diagnosed growth hormone deficiency, somatrogon supplies the hormone that stimulates growth at the growth plates, which raises annual growth rate in trials. Its practical difference from older products is the weekly schedule. Height effects are documented in deficient, prepubertal children treated under specialist care.
